prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: B009 is the only candidate on which all eight openings agree: every member ranks it, six place it in the top three, and all eight propose the same two names. That convergence matters less to me than the substance. The magic-wavelength lattice is a genuine invention that removes the dominant systematic of a neutral-atom clock, and it was then taken to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 in strontium and ytterbium, confirmed independently in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere. The consequences are concrete: tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy, searches for new physics and the preparation for a redefinition of the second. The credit is also unusually clean for this list: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and many-body frontier. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize were about different steps, so this is a continuation of precision measurement rather than a repeat. From where I sit as an atomic theorist I can add that the clock transitions rest on carefully understood relativistic atomic structure, blackbody-shift and polarisability physics, which is part of why the performance claims are trustworthy.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is category: some colleagues may see a clock as precision engineering rather than a discovery, and the Academy has recently honoured frequency combs and ion clocks, so the lineage overlap is real. Credit beyond the two names (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat, PTB and NIST groups) is also not trivial, and a two-person prize leaves out the many-group character of the 1e-18 milestones. Finally, the decisive consumer of these clocks, the redefinition of the second, has not happened yet, so some of the scientific payoff is still prospective. I judge these concerns real but not decisive, because the invention is clear and the confirmation is overwhelming.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B009 first as measurement physics whose reach is set by how accurately one can measure, and discloses that Ye trained in John Hall's laboratory, where he spent a research period; he stresses that the Katori-Ye pairing is fair and that other groups contributed demonstrations but not the founding idea.
responses.response: I agree on the scientific case and on the pairing, and I appreciate the disclosure. I would add that the Hall connection is a reason for the committee to look closely at the lineage question rather than to discount the candidate: the comb gave the ruler, but the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate idea that removed the Doppler and light-shift limits for neutral atoms, so I do not think B009 is a rerun of 2005. Where I am more cautious than Kroll is on his move to pair B001 as a close second; atom interferometry has a tangled 1991 priority picture and a 1997 laureate in the lineage, and I would not let it compete with B009 on credit clarity.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, openly noting his own field and Chalmers/WACQT proximity, and argues that B008 is distinct from the 2025 macroscopic-tunnelling prize while worrying about another circuit award so soon.
responses.response: I take the distinctness argument seriously, and I ranked B008 fifth myself because circuit QED is architecturally foundational. But your own two reservations are the ones that keep me from putting it first: the closeness to 2025 and the unsettled position of Wallraff and Devoret in the credit. A three-name prize of Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf is defensible, but it is more exposed to a credit dispute than the Katori-Ye pair. I would also say that an award which leaves the field that won in 2025 untouched for a few years is not a penalty to circuit QED, only sequencing, and B009 has no such sequencing problem.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a detector-driven opening of neutrino astronomy and argues that the decisive pair is Halzen and Karle, with Spiering and the precursor projects complicating a fair three-person split.
responses.response: I think the discovery is real and the instrumental achievement impressive, and I accept that the diffuse-flux claim is stable. My difficulty is credit and framing: within the supplied names you yourself say the allocation is unsettled, the collaboration is several hundred strong, and the origin of most of the flux is still open, so the prize citation would have to choose between concept, detection and sources. I could support a two-name Halzen-Karle version if that were the committee's direction, but B009 gives us a cleaner, better-confirmed object today. I would keep B052 in view for a later year rather than push it ahead of the clocks.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B009 first with B010 second, stressing that the lattice-clock idea and its statistical-metrology payoff are crisp, and that Zoller's credit overlaps between the optical-lattice simulation candidate and the Cirac-Zoller candidate.
responses.response: I share both points. On B009 we are closely aligned. On B010 my reservation is the same as yours: four credited names, at most three laureates, and Zoller sitting in both B010 and B014, so any prize combining them needs an explicit decision about where his credit is recognised. I hold B010 at fourth because the Bloch-Greiner-Esslinger experiments are strong but the allocation is contestable, and I think the committee should resolve B014 versus B010 as one question rather than two.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first and topological insulators second, treating B018 as complementary to the 2016 topological-phases prize, and ranks B009 fifth as a strong instrumental discovery and natural continuation of the comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I agree with you on B018 being complementary to 2016 and I ranked it second myself; if the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize this year, I would support Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as my preferred alternative. Where we differ is the weight on B009: you call it a strong instrumental discovery, and I would say the invention of the magic-wavelength lattice is the kind of conceptual step that the 'discovery or invention' criterion is meant to reward, not only a record in accuracy. The BHZ and 3D topological-insulator omissions make B018 a harder prize to write fairly than B009.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock as a discovery-class invention or as metrology instrumentation overlapping the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether a two-name Katori-Ye prize would be seen as underweighting the other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, PTB, NIST).
If B018 were preferred instead, how to treat the omitted BHZ and three-dimensional topological-insulator contributors.
How the committee would handle Zoller across B010 and B014 if both remained in contention.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B009 from my profile: Katori and Ye are not among the collaborators it documents. I disclose general proximity: I am an atomic theorist with documented collaborations with the Lund attosecond group (including Anne L'Huillier) and with Ursula Keller's group at ETH, and I worked with Luca Argenti, J. Marcus Dahlstrom, Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato; none of these is a credited name on the shortlist. Because B009, B014 and B010 lie in my own broad field of atomic physics, I flag a disciplinary bias that I cannot fully correct for.
